messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Dr. García had always been a man of precision and control, both in his personal life and in the operating room where he spent most of his days as a surgeon. But all of that changed one fateful night when he was involved in a severe car accident on his way home from a late shift at the hospital. The sound of screeching tires, the crunch of metal, and the feeling of weightlessness still haunted him to this day. As he recovered from his physical injuries, Dr. García began to notice that certain things would trigger memories of the accident. Seeing his loved ones, particularly his wife and children, would bring back vivid images of what could have been if he hadn't made it out alive. The texture of the airbag that had deployed during the crash also seemed to be seared into his memory, and even the slightest touch of something similar would transport him back to that moment. And then there were the cars – every time he saw a vehicle that had been involved in an accident, his mind would flash back to the wreckage of his own car. At first, Dr. García tried to push these memories away, but they seemed to have a life of their own. They would force their way into his mind at the most inopportune moments, leaving him feeling shaken and disoriented. He found himself avoiding certain situations that might trigger these memories – he stopped taking his usual route home from work, which passed by the scene of the accident, and he even began to avoid spending time with his loved ones, fearing that their presence would bring back the traumatic memories. As the months went by, Dr. García started to notice that he was also avoiding activities that brought him joy. He used to love playing golf on the weekends, but now the thought of it seemed too overwhelming. He felt like he couldn't enjoy himself without being reminded of what had happened, and so he just stopped trying. He also began to avoid any situation that might put his body under physical stress – no more intense workouts or long hikes. It was as if he was waiting for the other shoe to drop, for something else bad to happen. But even with all these avoidance strategies in place, the memories still lingered. They felt more real than normal memories, and Dr. García couldn't shake the feeling that they were somehow more important. He would catch himself thinking about the accident at random moments, reliving the fear and the panic. And yet, whenever he tried to fully recall the details of what had happened, something inside him would push back, blocking out the memory before it could surface. As a result, Dr. García felt like he was living in a state of constant hypervigilance, always on the lookout for potential triggers that might send him spiraling back into the past. His relationships with his loved ones began to suffer – they didn't understand why he was pushing them away, and Dr. García couldn't explain it himself. He felt like he was losing himself in the process of trying to avoid the memories, but he didn't know how else to cope. It wasn't until his wife sat him down one day and told him that she couldn't take it anymore – that she needed her husband back – that Dr. García realized just how much he had been avoiding. He was afraid of losing control, afraid of being overwhelmed by the memories and the emotions that came with them. But most of all, he was afraid of never being able to find his way back to himself. With a newfound sense of determination, Dr. García made the decision to seek help – not just for his own sake, but for the sake of those who loved him.
